ProbableCause: The elevator control restriction was caused by the failure of an elevator autopilot servo control cable which failed due to cyclic fatigue. The slack in the cable wrapped around the servo mount in such a way that it interfered with the rotation of the servo mount. The servo mount remained connected to the aft side of the elevator control quadrant by the intact aft cables. This condition resulted in the limited rotation of the elevator control quadrant in one direction.
AnalysisNarrative:
On November 23, 2025, about 0950 central standard time (CST), SkyWest Airlines flight 4229, an MHIRJ Aviation Group CL-600-2C11 (CRJ550), N707EV, experienced a restriction in nose-up pitch control during the flare while landing at Range Regional Airport (KHIB), Hibbing, Minnesota. Despite the control issue, the airplane touched down and taxied to the gate with no further issues. The flight was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 121 scheduled domestic flight from Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport (KMSP), St. Paul, MN to KHIB. There were no injuries to occupants and there was no damage to the aircraft.
SkyWest Airlines maintenance found that the elevator autopilot servo control cable (part number BA670-93710-13) was broken, and that the slack in the broken cable was wrapped around the autopilot servo mount in such a way that it caused the pitch restriction. Previous events investigated by the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) (see NTSB Investigation Number ENG25LA009) found that when this cable fails, the slack in the broken cable bound between the elevator autopilot servo mount and the cable guide pins. The bound cable interfered with the rotation of the servo mount, which remained connected to the aft side of the elevator control quadrant by the intact aft cables. This condition resulted in the limited rotation of the elevator control quadrant in one direction.
The broken cable was sent to the NTSB Materials Laboratory for further examination. The construction of the cable was 7x7 and made from carbon steel. The fracture occurred 14 inches from the elevator autopilot servo mount end. Examination revealed that the individual wires near the fracture were worn and exhibited features consistent with cyclic fatigue. SkyWest Airlines reported that the airplane had accrued 44,643 flight hours and 33,624 flight cycles at the time of the cable failure. The cable was last inspected per MRB Task 273000-201A in May of 2016, 11,915 flight hours prior to the failure. SkyWest Airlines stated that the cable had not been replaced since they acquired the airplane in June of 2020.
Additional Reported Cable Failures
On January 31, 2026, SkyWest Airlines maintenance personnel found the elevator autopilot servo control cable (part number BA670-93710-13) broken on a CRJ700 (registration number N707SK). The report that prompted maintenance to troubleshoot the airplane stated that greater than normal elevator back pressure was needed to control aircraft pitch. The airplane had accrued 51,171 flight hours and 34,606 flight cycles at the time of the cable failure. The cable was last inspected per MRB Task 273000-201A in April 2025, 1,802 flight hours before the failure occurred. SkyWest Airlines stated that the cable had not been replaced since they acquired the airplane in May of 2005. The NTSB did not request the failed cable for laboratory analysis due to its similarities with the incident cable failure and the failures documented in NTSB Investigation Number ENG25LA009.
Corrective Actions
MHIRJ released service bulletins SB 670BA-27-078 and SB 601R-27-167, both dated 01 October 2025, to provide instruction to replace the affected cables on CRJ 200/550/700/900/1000 based on accrued flight hours of the cables. Transport Canada released Airworthiness Directive number CF-2025-63 with effective date of 1 December 2025 to mandate compliance with the MHIRJ service bulletins. The Federal Aviation Administration released Airworthiness Directive number 2026-02-03 with effective date of 5 February 2026 to require replacing the elevator autopilot servo control cables on affected airplanes.
InvestigationClass: Class 4 - Basic report with no Prelim publish

ProbableCause: United Airlines flight crew’s failure to maintain adequate clearance from the parked Envoy Airlines airplane while taxiing in winter weather conditions.
AnalysisNarrative:
The accident occurred when the left wingtip of United Airlines flight 2333 (UA2333), N480UA, an Airbus A320-232 collided with the right horizontal stabilizer and elevator of Envoy Airlines flight 4028 (ENY4028), N317TB, an Embraer ERJ-175 (which was stationary) while taxiing to the gate after landing at Chicago O’Hare International Airport (ORD), Chicago, Illinois. There were no reported injuries to passengers or crew on either airplane. ENY4028 sustained substantial damage to its elevator and horizontal stabilizer (Figure 1) and UA2333 sustained minor damage to its left winglet.

      
Figure 1. Left photo shows damage to ENY4028 right horizontal stabilizer and the right photo shows the damaged right elevator. (Source: Envoy Airlines)
Statements from the Envoy Airlines flight crew indicated that ORD was experiencing a winter weather storm with heavy snow falling for several hours and the taxiways were covered in snow making the taxi center lines difficult to see. Statements from the United Airlines flight crew also indicated that the taxiways were completely snow-covered, obscuring centerlines, taxiway edges, and several taxiway signs.

According to the Envoy Airlines flight crew, flight ENY4028 conducted a single-engine taxi from gate L20 to runway 9R with engine No. 1 (left) operating, and auxiliary power unit (APU) in use. The airplane was taxiing northbound on taxiway U, when the flight crew attempted to turn the airplane left onto taxiway K. As the airplane started the left turn, it began to skid. The captain applied the brakes to prevent further movement and asked the first officer (FO) to start the No. 2 (right) engine in an attempt to regain control. While the FO started the engine, the captain informed air traffic control (ATC) of their situation and requested and received approval to remain stopped while they attempted to reposition the aircraft. Shortly thereafter, the flight crew felt the airplane being struck by an external object, and the nose moved from right to left about 5°. The FO looked to the right and observed a United Airlines Airbus that had just taxied behind them and continued forward.

According to statements from the United Airlines flight crew, they conducted an uneventful landing on runway 9C and proceeded to taxi toward gate C26, with reported visibility of ¼ mile with heavy snowfall. Once northbound on taxiway U, they observed ENY4028 attempting to make a left turn onto taxiway K. During the turn, the airplane appeared to slide slightly before continuing forward and then stopping. The flight crew elected to hold their position initially since ENY4028 appeared to partially block their path. 

Once they were stationary, the captain visually cleared the left side of the airplane, and the FO visually cleared the right side of the airplane, and a sidestep maneuver was performed. The FO indicted that he verified verbally with the captain that they had clearance around the ENY4028. The captain confirmed. The flight crew indicated that they taxied forward at a very slow speed due to the restricted visibility and degraded taxiway conditions, closely monitoring the left wingtip for clearance. They observed their left wing pass the tailpipe of ENY4028 without issue. Shortly thereafter, they experienced a slight vibration. Their initial assessment was that they may have run over accumulated snow or debris on the taxiway, so they continued toward the gate.

Ground control advised UA2333 that another airplane reported possible contact with them from behind and asked whether they had noticed anything. UA2333’s flight crew advised ground control of experiencing a vibration. They asked ground control whether they preferred they stop or continue to the gate and were instructed to continue and advise of any observed damage. They arrived at the gate, deplaned normally, immediately contacted maintenance, and wrote an entry into the logbook. After the flight crew walked outside, they noticed the lower left winglet was damaged.

The automated weather reported at ORD at 1424 included visibility of ¼ statute mile in heavy snow and freezing fog. 

The impact between UA2333 left winglet and ENY4028 tail resulted in a fractured winglet for UA2333 and damage to the ENY4028 right horizontal stabilizer and elevator.  ENY4028’s elevator sustained a fractured tip cap and deformation to the trailing edge outboard end.  ENY4028’s right horizontal stabilizer had a puncture about 20 inches long by 4 inches wide with fracture damage and deformation to the skin, 3 stringers and 1 rib. This damage adversely affected the structural strength and flight characteristics requiring a major repair or replacement and was considered substantial. The damage to the UAL2333 left winglet was considered minor.

ProbableCause: The flight crew’s improper derotation which resulted in a hard nose gear touchdown.  Contributing to the accident was the captain and first officer’s lack of crew resource management related to communication about pitch control inputs.  Contributing to the improper derotation, was the crew’s lack of situational awareness about the control yoke inputs during landing.  This resulted in the captain’s restriction of the control yoke aft movement and the first officer losing his grip on the control yoke, which led to an uncontrolled nose down pitch movement and subsequent hard touchdown of the nose landing gear.
AnalysisNarrative:
Air Transport International (ATI) cargo flight 4340 experienced a hard landing at San Bernadino International Airport (SBD), San Bernadino, California. The unscheduled domestic cargo flight was operated under the provisions of Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 121 from Spokane International Airport (GEG), Spokane, Washington. The airplane sustained substantial damage and there were no injuries. 
A postaccident examination of the airplane performed by the operator revealed damage to the crown of the upper fuselage. The fuselage skin was buckled and fractured, as shown in figure 1, with damage to the underlying stringers, lap and butt joints. 


Figure 1. Fuselage damage on top and right side. (Source: ATI)
The flight crew noted no anomalies with the airplane before or during flight. The first officer was the pilot flying. They performed a comprehensive approach briefing for the ILS to runway 6. They checked the automated terminal information system (ATIS) which indicated no concerning weather, with “excellent” VFR conditions and light winds. The airplane intercepted the localizer about 12 miles out, and they both described the approach as stable. 
The first officer disconnected the autopilot between 250 and 200 ft above the ground as planned. As he heard the automated radio altitude callouts for 50 ft and 40ft, he began to reduce the decent rate, and at 10 ft, he retarded the throttles and prepared for touch down. He recalled the touchdown being normal, and then recognized the nose tended to pitch up. He relaxed the control column and applied forward pressure to prevent further pitch up. “At that moment, the controls moved forward abruptly and forcefully”, which caused him to momentarily lose his grip on the controls. 
The nosewheel then forcefully contacted the runway. Afterwards, the airplane went back to a steady condition, and he applied left rudder to maintain centerline. At 60 knots, the captain called “my controls” and the first officer transferred the controls to him. The remainder of the rollout and taxi were uneventful. 
The captain recalled that the landing flare was initiated at the appropriate time, though (at some time) he noticed “what appeared to be an over-rotation causing the plane to balloon.” Concerned about the “high pitch attitude and trend” [and the potential for a tail strike], he stuck his hand out to block the yoke from coming back further. The airplane then “de-rotated rapidly, landing with a jarring impact.” 
A review of the flight data and cockpit voice recorder readouts revealed that the airplane had initially touched down (air/ground indication of “ground” and sound similar to wheels contacting runway) at an airspeed of about 124 knots, flaps 25°, with a pitch attitude of about 5° nose up, and a control column position of about +12° (positive values are aft of neutral). About 1-2 seconds later, the air ground indication momentarily changed to “air” for a single sample (recorded at 1 second intervals) and then back to “ground” where it remained. 
Between the two “ground” indications, the control column position reduced to about +6°, and the pitch attitude reduced to about 3°. Just after the second “ground” indication, the control column position increased to about +20° and then immediately reversed and decreased to about -20° (negative values are forward of neutral). The decrease occurred over about 1.5 seconds, and during that time the CVR recorded an utterance from the first officer. 
Further, during this aft-then-forward control column sequence, the airspeed initially decreased from about 119 to 113 knots, and the pitch attitude increased from about 3° to about 6°, before it decreased to about 0°. This decrease was the derotation to nose landing gear touchdown. As the pitch attitude reached 0°, a large spike in vertical acceleration was recorded (upwards to about 1.6 Gs, then reversed to about 0.1 Gs), consistent with nose landing gear touchdown.  
While the first officer recalled that the controls moved abruptly forward while he was at the same time already moving it forward, the captain recalled putting his hand up to prevent further movement of the control column aft. The investigation was unable to resolve this discrepancy definitively. However, they both recalled that the derotation occurred just after their respective actions (the blocking of aft movement by the captain, and the loss of grip on the yoke of the first officer).  That interaction almost certainly occurred during the +20° to -20° control column sequence, because that sequence ended with the derotation. It may have happened just prior to the first officer’s utterance captured by the CVR.  See figure 2. 

Figure 2. Chart of FDR and CVR data during landing. 
The captain’s concern about a possible trail strike was likely due to the airplane’s pitch attitude which increased after touchdown and had ultimately reached about 6° nose up. Geometrically, the tail should strike ground at a pitch attitude of about 8° nose up with the main landing gear compressed (see NTSB accident investigation DCA25LA085). The airplane manufacturer’s flight crew training manual advises that pilots should not allow the pitch attitude to increase, or to hold the nose wheel off the runway after landing, which could lead to a tail strike. 
However, there was no verbal communication between the crew recorded on the CVR at the time of the captain’s intervention, or the first officer’s loss of grip on the yoke. According to the crew’s statements, as well as conversations captured by the CVR after landing (between the captain and first officer, as well as of the captain while on a telephone call), the crew did not realize at the time what exactly had occurred. 
The first officer didn’t realize that the captain had restricted the aft column motion, and the captain, who was looking at the runway at the time, didn’t see that the first officer’s hands had slipped off the yoke. They discovered this during their after-landing conversations, and concluded that for a period of time, apparently neither one of them were on the controls. The review of the recorded data could not definitively confirm when, or for how long the pilots had their hands off the control yoke.
However, it is likely that it began near or after the time that the control column reached its peak value of about 20° aft (because the captain was trying to limit its aft travel) and likely continued through the nose down control column trend at least until the time the pitch attitude reached 0° and the large vertical acceleration was recorded. The manufacturer’s flight crew training manual also advises not to make large nose-down control column movements, to avoid structural damage.
Derotation is the lowering of the aircraft’s nose gear to the runway following touchdown on the main gear during landing. In a review of National Transportation Safety Board investigations and assisted international investigations, eight similar derotation accidents involving Boeing 757/767 aircraft were found. Those investigations were: 
January 16, 1992 - Asiana Airlines in Cheu Island, South Korea 
October 27, 1992 – American Airlines flight 957 in São Paulo, Brazil 
December 31, 1993 – LOT flight 002 in Warsaw, Poland 
July 31, 1997 – Federal Express in Newark, New Jersey 
May 22, 2002 – Monarch Airlines in Gibraltar 
April 20, 2009 – Royal Air Maroc flight 200 in New York, New York 
August 18, 2019 – Delta Air Lines 414 in Ponta Delgada, Portugal
July 29, 2023 – United Airlines 702 in Houston, Texas.  
These accidents occurred when the pilots applied large nose-down control column deflections after main landing gear touchdown, which resulted in large nose-down pitch rates and high vertical velocities at the nose gear. It was this combination of vertical velocity and pitch rate that resulted in compression loads

ProbableCause: The reduced surface friction of the contaminated ramp which led to a loss of directional control during taxi.
AnalysisNarrative:
Alaska Airlines cargo flight 9623 from Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport (ANC), Anchorage, Alaska to Kodiak Airport (ADQ), Kodiak, Alaska collided with two stationary baggage carts while taxiing on the contaminated (slush, ice and water) ramp at ADQ. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the aft right cargo door and frame. There were no injuries. 

According to the flight crew, the airplane landed uneventfully on runway 26, then taxied to the ramp via taxiway F. They reported the braking action on the runway as good to medium, and that the brakes were effective while on taxiway F. 


Figure 1. Airport Diagram. (Source: Federal Aviation Administration) 

After turning left from taxiway F to the ramp, the captain noticed that “eventually the braking action went to nil” and when he attempted to stop, the airplane weather vaned (nose to the left) and struck the ground equipment at the airplane’s right rear side. 


Figure 2. Damage to cargo door. (Source: Alaska Airlines)

The reported accident time was 1253 Alaska Standard Time. The weather reported at ADQ at the time of the accident included moderate rain and mist, temperature 39° F, and wind from 120° at 15 knots with gusts to 25 knots. Field condition reports (FICONs), provided in Notices To Airmen for ADQ, described the condition of different surfaces around the airport. The flight crew had these FICONs, however the most recently available reports were issued several hours prior to the accident, including: 

At 0531, all of the apron/ramp area was described as having 2 inches of wet snow; 
At 0715, taxiway F contained ice;
At 0825, runway 26 was described as 100 percent of the surface being wet.

The flight crew reported that at the time of the accident, the ramp surface initially appeared as though it had “a lot of slush.” After the airplane came to a stop, they noticed standing water over ice on the ramp. The flight crew had a difficult time walking on the ramp and requested sand be spread in the area between the airplane and the terminal.

ProbableCause: The first officer’s excessive aft sidestick input combined with decaying airspeed during initiation of a go-around, resulting in an increase in the airplane pitch attitude and subsequent lower fuselage contacting the runway.
AnalysisNarrative:
JetBlue Airways flight 2233 experienced a tailstrike while attempting to land on runway 28L at San Francisco International Airport (SFO), San Francisco, California. The scheduled domestic passenger flight was operated under the provisions of Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 121. The airplane sustained substantial damage and there were no injuries to the 6 crew and 148 passengers onboard.
According to the flight crew, the final approach and landing were uneventful, and the winds were described as “light”. The first officer (FO), who was the pilot flying, recalled the left main landing gear touched down before the right main landing gear and believed they encountered minor wake turbulence from the departing aircraft. The captain, who was the pilot monitoring, recalled the main landing gear touching down normally. The FO stated the airplane did not settle toward the runway as expected, at which point the FO decided to initiate a go-around because he was unsure if they would complete the transition to landing within the first 3,000 ft of runway. The captain shifted his attention during touchdown from the outside to the lower navigation display, then back to outside when the FO called out the go-around. The FO recalled feeling a “thud” during initiation of the go-around. The second approach and landing onto runway 28L at SFO was accomplished without incident. 
Postlanding inspection of the airplane by the captain revealed substantial damage to the lower fuselage consistent with its contact with the runway. There was no reported mechanical malfunction that contributed to excessive airplane pitch angle when the airplane touched down on the runway. The recorded flight data showed the airplane bounced after initial touchdown. About 3 seconds later, the FO sidestick parameter showed a full aft input, for a duration of 2 seconds, while the engine throttles advanced to takeoff/go-around (TOGA) power and the main landing gear was still contacting the ground. The airplane’s pitch angle increased from 5.4° to 11° during the 2-second full aft sidestick input, and the airplane’s pitch angle further increased and peaked at 15.4° two seconds later while the airplane was still in close proximity to the ground. During this timeframe, airspeed decayed to about 12 knots below the target approach speed during the full aft sidestick input before airspeed began to increase. 
The operator’s flight crew procedures for a bounce at touchdown include the instructions “do not allow the pitch attitude to increase…” and for a low bounce, the pilot should maintain pitch attitude and complete the landing while keeping the thrust at idle. Furthermore, for a high bounce, if the safe outcome of a bounce is in question, to maintain the pitch attitude and apply TOGA thrust. The anti-tailstrike protection feature of the airplane flight control system, which limits commanded pitch rate after touchdown, deactivated as designed when TOGA power was selected. The FO likely did not detect the bounce at touchdown based on their full aft sidestick input during initiation of the go-around, leading to a large increase in airplane pitch angle before the airplane climbed, resulting in a tailstrike.

ProbableCause: The captain’s inadequate compensation for gusting crosswind wind conditions while attempting to land and a subsequent go-around.
AnalysisNarrative:
Endeavor Air, Inc. doing business as, Delta Connection, flight 5304, a Mitsubishi Heavy Industries RJ Aviation (formerly Bombardier) CL-600-2C10 (CRJ700), sustained minor damage to both wingtips while attempting to land at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), Atlanta, Georgia.
According to the flight crew, the departure and enroute portions of the flight were uneventful. After completing the approach briefing and descent checklist, air traffic control instructed the flight to descend via the HOBTT3 Arrival. While descending through 10,000 ft mean sea level (msl), the crew encountered light turbulence and were instructed to expedite the descent through 4,000 ft msl. The flight was subsequently vectored and cleared for the instrument landing system (ILS) approach to runway 27L. During the approach, about 2,000 ft msl, the first officer (FO), who was serving as pilot monitoring, reported the runway in sight.
Through 1,000 ft msl, the turbulence intensified and the captain, who was the pilot flying, disconnected the autopilot. About 100 ft above ground level (agl), the first officer called “Vref plus 10,” and the captain made a minor power adjustment. About 30 ft above the runway’s surface, during the flare, the airplane encountered a gust of wind and ballooned. The airplane then rolled to the right, and the captain initiated a go-around. While attempting to level the wings, he overcontrolled, resulting in the left wing contacting the runway. He subsequently overcontrolled in the opposite direction, resulting in the right wing contacting the ground. Following the go-around, the first officer assumed control and completed an uneventful landing.
A surface weather observation taken about 22 minutes after the incident reported wind from 230° at 14 knots, with gusts to 23 knots. With a peak gust reported about 20 minutes before the incident from 210° at 30 knots.

ProbableCause: The tug drivers improper positioning of the airplane during pushback, which resulted in the airplane’s jet blast impacting an active gate area during taxi and the subsequent injury to a maintenance technician. Contributing to the accident was the captain’s decision to accept the tug driver’s incorrect release location.
AnalysisNarrative:
On March 24, 2026, about 1815 eastern daylight time (EDT), United Airlines flight 1303, was involved in an accident while taxiing for departure at Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD), Dulles, Virginia. The 167 passengers and crew onboard were uninjured. One maintenance technician was seriously injured. The flight was operating under Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 121 as a regularly scheduled domestic passenger flight from IAD to Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA), Seattle, Washington. 
According to the flight crew, preflight preparations were normal, and no abnormalities were observed with either the airplane or ground personnel. The airplane was parked at Gate C6 between two aircraft undergoing preflight and post-flight activities. Departure was delayed several minutes to accommodate connecting international passengers. They were cleared to push back with the airplane's tail-oriented east to facilitate a westbound taxi on taxiway Echo (E), abeam Gate C8.
During the pushback, the tug driver made two unsuccessful attempts to properly position the airplane. A nearby ramp worker joined the right-wing walker on the headset communications and appeared to discuss the situation with the tug driver. The captain asked over the intercom if everything was alright. After receiving no response, he repeated the inquiry, and the tug driver advised that they would attempt to reposition the airplane one more time.
Following the final repositioning attempt, the airplane remained north of the taxiway E centerline on the terminal side. The flight crew was then instructed to set the parking brake. Before disconnecting the headset, the tug driver stated, "Sorry for the wonky pushback," to which the captain replied, "Glad you figured it out." The ground personnel then moved clear of the airplane, and the marshaller signaled that the area was clear. The captain acknowledged the signal by flashing the taxi light, indicating the airplane was ready to taxi.
Air traffic control subsequently cleared the flight to taxi via taxiways E, E2, and F to Spot 86. The captain advanced the thrust levers to breakaway thrust, and the airplane began taxiing. The remainder of the flight was uneventful.
According to the pushback driver, before brake release the flight crew instructed him to position the aircraft for a west taxiway departure and align it with taxiway C8. He stated that the pushback was unusual due to construction near gate C2 and the presence of widebody aircraft at adjacent gates. 
During the maneuver, he had difficulty achieving a 90-degree alignment and was concerned about over-rotating the nose gear. After several attempts, he repositioned the aircraft beyond gate C6 and asked the captain if the aircraft was in position for brake set. Following completion of the pushback, he observed a maintenance technician on the ground near gate C4 and summoned assistance.
United Airlines had issued Flight Operations, Ops Alert, Washington Dulles (IAD) Taxiway Echo Construction, Revision 1, that was effective and available to the pilots at the time of the accident (see figure 1). The Ops Alert stated in part: 
Why:
Beginning March 16, the Metropolitan Washington Airport Authority (MWAA) will continue the renovation of Taxiway E to support the Terminal 2 Extension (T2E) project. Construction hours are daily from 2100-1300L. This work will impact access to Gates C2 and C4, prevent entering Taxiway E from the East, and close Taxiway J between Taxiways E and F. 


Figure 1. Graphic included in United Airlines Flight Operations, Ops Alert, Washington Dulles (IAD) Taxiway Echo Construction, Revision 1. 
Airport surveillance video showed the airplane was not released from the tug at the designated location abeam Gate C8 on taxiway E, but rather about abeam Gate C6 and north of the taxiway E centerline. As the airplane began to taxi and turned to position on the taxiway centerline its jet blast was directed toward an airplane parked at Gate C4, see figure 2. Shortly thereafter, a ladder was observed sliding across the ramp’s surface behind the parked airplane's No. 2 (right) engine.

Figure 2. Pushback and taxi illustration based on surveillance video. The yellow dot indicates the approved drop location. (Source: United Airlines)
After the flight, the flight crew was informed that a maintenance technician had sustained serious injuries after falling from a ladder displaced by their airplane’s jet blast .
Safety Actions 
Since the accident, United Airlines has implemented the following mitigations to prevent recurrence:
A safety standdown was held in station regarding the proper push path related to this gate during the construction period with all pushback qualified personnel.
Policy related to the final positioning of aircraft, specifically, that an aircraft must be pushed to a location where jet blast can pose no harm to personnel or equipment was played on ramp information displays throughout employee areas of the station as a reminder of that policy.
A revised Ops Alert, requiring Mandatory 2 engine taxi was implemented for the duration of the construction to ensure that engine power settings are kept as low as reasonably practicable.
InvestigationClass: Class 4 - Basic report with no Prelim publish

ProbableCause: The airplane’s encounter with turbulence resulted in serious injuries to a flight attendant who was not seated due to completion of arrival compliance checks.
AnalysisNarrative:
JetBlue flight 1245, a scheduled domestic passenger flight from Long Island MacArthur Airport (ISP), Islip, New York to Palm Beach International Airport (PBI), West Palm Beach, Florida, encountered turbulence during descent into PBI. As a result, one flight attendant received serious injuries.
The first officer, the pilot flying, stated they entered a small cloud layer around 7,000 ft to 9,000 ft and encountered brief but sharp turbulence that lasted about 3 seconds. The flight attendants stated they had just completed their compliance checks and were securing the galley during the turbulence. One of the two aft flight attendants reported being thrown to the floor and required the assistance of the other aft flight attendant to get into their jump seat. 
Both aft flight attendants described the turbulence as “severe.” One of the forward flight attendants contacted the flight deck and reported to the captain that emergency medical services would be needed at the gate due to cabin crew injuries. The flight landed in PBI without further incident. The two forward flight attendants reported sustaining minor injuries. The aft flight attendant was taken to a local hospital for evaluation and was diagnosed with a fractured pelvis and vertebrae.
The captain and first officer reported seeing no significant returns on the onboard weather radar at the time that turbulence was encountered. The first officer stated they reported the turbulence to air traffic control, who also advised that their radar showed no significant weather activity in that sector. There were no significant meteorological information (SIGMET), convective SIGMETs, or Center Weather Advisories over the general flight route into PBI at the time of the accident. A pilot report (PIREP) around 15:30 local time reported severe turbulence during descent into PBI at 2,000 ft, but there were no relevant PIREPs at the time flight 1245 was descending into PBI.

ProbableCause: An unanticipated encounter with clear air turbulence while in cruise flight.
AnalysisNarrative:
On March 29, 2026, about 1456 pacific daylight time (PDT), United Airlines flight 115, encountered moderate turbulence while in cruise flight at FL300 en route to Faa’a (Tahiti) International Airport (NTAA) Papeete, French Polynesia. Of the 164 passengers and crew onboard, one flight attendant sustained a serious injury. The flight was operating under Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 121 as a regularly scheduled international passenger flight from San Francisco International Airport (SFO), San Francisco, California to NTAA. 
According to the flight crew, dispatch had planned the flight at FL300 due to forecast turbulence between FL320 and FL380 off the California coast. After departure, the flight attendants remained seated until the airplane reached cruise altitude at FL300 and conditions were deemed suitable to begin cabin service. During the first 90 minutes of flight, the airplane encountered intermittent light turbulence, resulting in multiple communications with dispatch and periodic illumination of the seatbelt sign. Dispatch advised that the greatest turbulence risk was expected between latitudes 34°N and 30°N.
About 95 minutes after departure, the airplane encountered a jolt of moderate clear air turbulence with no corresponding returns displayed at altitude on the onboard weather radar. The sudden encounter with moderate turbulence resulted in two flight attendants falling. The flight crew immediately directed the flight attendants to be seated and notified dispatch of the turbulence encounter. Dispatch advised that the airplane had recently crossed the subtropical jet stream, a condition unknown to the flight crew at the time. Shortly thereafter, the cockpit was informed that a flight attendant had been injured.
Following notification of the injury, the flight crew coordinated with dispatch and MedLink and requested emergency medical services to meet the airplane upon arrival. A physician traveling onboard evaluated the injured flight attendant and recommended diagnostic imaging upon landing. The flight attendant was subsequently transported to a hospital, where they were diagnosed with a serious injury.  
At the time of the flight’s turbulence encounter there were no active inflight weather advisories or company issued advisories for the area.

ProbableCause: The airplane’s encounter with turbulence during descent resulting in a serious injury to a flight attendant.
AnalysisNarrative:
Southwest Airlines flight 2392, operating between Chicago Midway International Airport (MDW), Chicago, Illinois and General Edward Lawrence Logan International Airport (BOS), Boston, Massachusetts encountered moderate turbulence while in descent to BOS. One flight attendant sustained a serious injury and three sustained minor injuries during the turbulence encounter. The aircraft continued to BOS and landed without further incident.
The captain was the pilot monitoring and the first officer was the pilot flying. Prior to the flight, the flight crew reviewed the dispatch release and weather forecasts, which indicated turbulence during departure and two weather systems enroute. The flight crew instructed the flight attendants (FA) to remain seated until the turbulence subsided. About 20 minutes into the flight, the flight crew coordinated with the FAs on timing of cabin service and agreed they would be seated if the flight encountered turbulence. 
While briefing the BOS approach, the flight crew observed that the weather conditions had deteriorated. The flight crew prepared for a Category III (CAT III) instrument landing, which would require a transfer of controls from the first officer to the captain. The flight crew did not anticipate turbulence during descent into BOS. While descending through 14,000 ft, the airplane encountered unexpected moderate turbulence, however, the flight crew recalled that nothing was depicted on the airplane’s weather radar at that time. The flight crew attempted to deviate from their course to avoid further turbulence, but they continued to encounter light to moderate turbulence.
At the time of the turbulence encounter, the FAs were preparing the cabin for landing. Two FAs, in the aft galley, were thrown into the air and then onto the floor. One of the forward FAs and a passenger assisted both injured FAs to passenger seats in the last row, then the forward FA took an aft jumpseat for landing. The flight crew requested emergency medical personnel meet the airplane at the gate. The landing was uneventful and both FAs were subsequently transported to the hospital. One FA was treated and released and the other diagnosed with a fractured left foot. The two other FAs reported minor injuries.
A National Weather Service Convective Significant Meteorological Information (SIGMET) was valid for an area about 75 miles west of the event location. SkyPath, a crowdsourced turbulence tracking tool for pilots, did not depict turbulence in the vicinity of the flight. The flight recorded a moderate turbulence event in SkyPath. The hourly meteorological aerodrome report (METAR) for Rhode Island T.F. Green International Airport (PVD), Warwick, Rhode Island, located about 4 miles east of the turbulence encounter, indicated that the cloud ceiling had descended from 11,000 ft above ground level (agl) to about 9,500 ft agl.

ProbableCause: The first officer’s excessive aft sidestick input following a bounced landing, and the line check pilot’s delayed remedial action, which resulted in an increase in the airplane’s pitch attitude and a subsequent tailstrike.
AnalysisNarrative:
Delta Air Lines flight 1181 experienced a tailstrike while attempting to land on runway 22 at Laguardia Airport (LGA), New York, New York. The scheduled domestic passenger flight was operated under the provisions of Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 121. The airplane sustained substantial damage and there were no injuries to the 6 crew and 188 passengers onboard. 
The captain, who was serving as the line check pilot (LCP), was providing operational experience (OE) training to the first officer (FO). The accident flight was their fourth leg together and the FO’s third as the pilot flying.
According to the flight crew, the captain instructed the FO to hand-fly the arrival. The autopilot was disconnected at approximately 18,000 ft, and the autothrottles were disconnected at about 10,000 ft. The captain reported that the FO flew the arrival well, with no notable altitude or airspeed deviations until the final approach.
During short final, the airplane's airspeed began to decrease below the target approach speed. The FO made a thrust adjustment; however, it was insufficient to arrest the airspeed decay. After the captain called out the airspeed deviation, the FO made an additional thrust correction. The flare was initiated slightly late, resulting in a firm touchdown and subsequent bounce. 
Following the bounce, the FO applied excessive aft sidestick input, and the airplane touched down a second time. The captain then assumed control of the airplane, lowered the nose, and initiated a go-around. After the go-around was established, the FO resumed control and completed a subsequent approach and landing without further incident.
The flight attendants notified the flight deck that they heard a loud scraping noise during the landing attempt. Postlanding inspection of the airplane by the flight crew revealed substantial damage to the lower fuselage consistent with its contact with the runway.
There was no reported mechanical malfunction that contributed to the excessive airplane pitch angle when the airplane touched down on the runway. The recorded flight data showed the airplane touched down at pitch angle of about 7° and a vertical acceleration of 1.91 gravitational force equivalent (g) and bounced. The airplane’s pitch angle increased to 10.02° before the left sidestick inputs associated with the go-around were recorded. The airplane’s longitudinal flight guidance mode changed to “Pitch GA” (pitch go-around) and the autothrust was engaged. 
The operator’s flight crew procedures for a bounced landing recovery include the instructions “hold or re-establish a normal landing attitude and add thrust as necessary to control the rate of descent. Thrust need not be added for a shallow bounce or skip. When a high hard bounce occurs initiate a go-around. Apply TOGA thrust and use normal go-around procedures. Do not allow the pitch attitude to increase…” 
Had the FO recognized the hard-bounce condition, promptly initiated a go-around, and not allowed the pitch to increase in accordance with company procedures, or had the LCP intervened sooner and assumed control to execute the bounced-landing recovery, the excessive pitch attitude and subsequent tailstrike likely would have been avoided.

ProbableCause: An encounter with convectively induced turbulence during cruise flight in an area of forecast thunderstorm activity.
AnalysisNarrative:
On July 16, 2026, about 1502 eastern daylight time, SkyWest Airlines, operating as Delta Connection flight 3723, encountered severe turbulence while in cruise flight at FL370 en route to Hartsfield/Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), Atlanta, Georgia. Of the 71 passengers and crew members aboard, one flight attendant sustained a serious injury. The flight was operating under 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 121 as a regularly scheduled international passenger flight from North Eleuthera Airport (ELH), North Eleuthera, Bahamas, to ATL.
According to the flight crew, after departure they received an instrument flight rules (IFR) clearance to ATL with an initial climb to FL230, followed by FL340. During the climb, they encountered light turbulence associated with nearby cloud tops and requested a higher altitude to improve ride quality. The flight was subsequently cleared to FL360. After turning northbound, air traffic control (ATC) asked if they would prefer FL350 or FL370; the crew accepted FL370. The flight then continued in smooth air for about 50 minutes.
As the flight progressed, the flight crew observed cumulonimbus clouds along the route of flight and requested a deviation to the right. Flight attendants (FA) were advised of the potential for turbulence and told to use caution. While the fasten seat belt sign remained illuminated. ATC was unable to approve the request but authorized a deviation to the left. After completing the deviation, the flight was cleared direct SHRKS.
About 6 minutes later, the airplane encountered severe turbulence that lasted approximately 5 seconds. The flight crew reported no visual indications of impending turbulence from the flight deck and no corresponding returns on the onboard weather radar. During the encounter, the airplane experienced a loss of airspeed and activation of the stick shaker. The captain called "upset" and initiated recovery procedures. The airplane lost about 300 to 400 ft before recovery was completed and cruise flight at FL370 was resumed. 
At the time of the turbulence encounter, the forward flight attendant was in the forward galley after completing cabin service. During the turbulence encounter, she braced herself and then took her jumpseat. Following the encounter, passengers requested assistance after observing the aft flight attendant lying on the rear galley floor, having reportedly struck her head during the turbulence encounter. The forward flight attendant solicited assistance from medically qualified passengers, who evaluated and assisted the injured flight attendant. She subsequently notified the flight crew of the injury and checked for additional passenger injuries.
After receiving notification of the injury, the flight crew coordinated with company dispatch and diverted to Jacksonville International Airport (JAX), Jacksonville, Florida, where emergency medical services met the airplane upon arrival. The FA was subsequently transported to a hospital and was diagnosed with a serious injury.
At the time of the turbulence encounter the National Weather Service (NWS) Aviation Weather Center had issued a Convective Significant Meteorological Information (SIGMET) for an area of thunderstorms moving from 340° at 5 knots, with tops above FL450 for the area. In addition, a Center Weather Advisory was also issued for an area of embedded thunderstorms with tops to FL420, with moderate to heavy precipitation over northern Florida and southern Georgia. 
A review of meteorological and satellite information indicated that the route of flight was over an area of rapidly developing thunderstorms, with echoes and very strong updraft potential which likely caused the convectively induced turbulence (CIT) encounter. The echoes under the flight path rapidly rose through the aircraft’s altitude immediately following the turbulence encounter and cloud-to-ground lightning was detected in the immediate vicinity.
